newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Africa drive pays off for Standard Bank.
newsitem.headline: Africa drive pays off for Standard Bank.

text.p: A four-year push into the volatile African market has paid off for South Africa's Standard Bank group which is bullish about prospects after securing a foothold across a continent long seen as a no-go zone.

Graeme Bell, senior general manager of Standard's African Banking Group, said his unit now accounted for five percent of Standard Bank Investment Corp Ltd's total assets and 10 percent of attributable earnings.
The bank is represented in 14 countries with 77 branches, making it the largest in Africa. Its expansion drive began in 1992 with the acquisition of ANZ Grindlays' African interests.
"I'm delighted to say that from year one we were in the black in terms of our investment in Africa," Bell said in an interview with Reuters Financial Television.
"As I see it, we should have another good year in Africa this year."

Bell said the group had been determined to go into Africa following South Africa's moves towards democracy which started in the early 1990s, adding its drive had now paid off with a renewed interest from other banks.

"We have noticed a rekindling of interest in Africa from some of our major competitors...There is no doubt Africa is a huge market, but you have to show long-term commitment. It is not a continent you can come into on a short-term plan."
Looking ahead, Bell said the Standard group wanted to consolidate its gains before seeking further acquisitions.
But he rated Angola as a priority market.
"However, things need to settle there a bit before we decide in which way we are going to enter the market there," he added.
"Other than Angola, I would say our philosophy at the moment is to consolidate in Africa."
Bell said factors which had dented Africa's reputation included risks in politics, volatility of markets and, primarily, operating risks such as fraud.
Despite varying efficiency levels, and the requirement for patience and resilience, Africa was a good portfolio investment, Bell said.
"But you know we are Africans. So we are used to the marketplace and I think what may frighten other people off doesn't necessarily have the same effect on us," he said.
